title: Nothing in Your Pitch Ever Goes Wrong
book: Story: Substance, Structure, Style and the Principles of Screenwriting
author: Robert McKee
wiifm: Every pitch to a lender, every page explaining a debt solution, every presentation on placement is a story, usually told badly. Today you follow Robert McKee, a Detroit child actor who became the most famous and most mocked screenwriting teacher in the world, and who was played on screen as a bellowing guru in a film that mocked him. His book is the most rigorous manual on how stories work. You will learn why audiences only pay attention when something goes wrong, why your opposition makes you look strong, and how to turn a list of facts into something people feel.

ch.h: A boy on a Detroit stage
b: Robert McKee was born in Detroit in January 1941. As a boy he was put on stage in a local theatre production, and he kept acting all through his school years. He learned early, from the inside, the thing he would spend his life teaching: an audience sits still only while it wants to know what happens next.

He went to the University of Michigan, studied English and theatre, and later began a doctorate in cinema arts that he never finished. In between he worked as an actor and director in New York theatre, learning the craft scene by scene in front of paying audiences who would leave if they were bored.
Remember that unfinished doctorate. McKee was always a practitioner first and a scholar second, and that is both the strength of his book and the source of the criticism it has drawn.
ch.cap: A Detroit boy holds the audience: what happens next?

b: In the late nineteen-seventies McKee moved to Los Angeles to write for film and television. He sold some work, but his real gift turned out to be explaining why stories worked. In 1983 he began teaching a course at the University of Southern California, and it grew into his Story Seminar: three or four days in a hotel ballroom, hundreds of people in the room, and a large, ferocious man pacing and lecturing about structure from morning to night.
The seminar went around the world. Writers, producers, novelists and later business executives paid to sit through it. In 1997 he set the whole course down in a book, Story.

The book opens with a defence against the charge that he reduced art to a formula. Story, he writes, is about principles, not rules. A rule says you must do it this way. A principle says this works and has done through all remembered time. Whether he always lives up to that is a fair question, as we will see. But you are not reading him to write a screenplay. You are reading him because every attempt to make someone care about something is a story, usually told by people who have never studied stories.

His manner became part of the legend. He was blunt, theatrical and impatient with vague thinking, and students left either converted or furious. But what they took away was not a set of slogans. It was a vocabulary for diagnosing why a story was not working, and that is what the book offers you too.
ch.cap: Hundreds in a hotel ballroom; McKee paces and roars

b: If you take one idea from today, take this one. A character wants something. They take an action to get it, based on a belief about how the world will respond. Then the world responds differently, usually worse and always more powerfully than they expected. McKee calls the rift between what was expected and what actually happened the gap, and it is where story lives.

Now the character must act again, with better information and more at risk, and the gap opens again, wider. Meaning is only produced where the world refuses. A character who gets exactly what they expect has revealed nothing and learned nothing.

This explains why most pitches are dull. In a typical pitch, you have a plan, you carry it out, and it works. Every line goes up and to the right. Nothing ever surprises you. So there is nothing for an audience's attention to hold, because attention is not caught by competence. It is caught by the difference between what was expected and what happened.

Try it. Instead of listing your capabilities, tell one gap: we assumed the delay was in underwriting, we spent months proving it wasn't, and it turned out to be the paperwork all along. Attention holds because the listener wants to know what happened. And you have shown that you learned something hard, which is the only lasting reason for anyone to pay you rather than someone cheaper.

Notice, too, that McKee does not mean an artificial twist bolted on for effect. The gap must arise from the character's own choices and the world's honest response to them. A pitch that invents a crisis to seem exciting will be smelt out. A pitch that admits a real surprise and what it taught you will be believed.
ch.cap: Expectation runs straight on; the world opens a gap

b: McKee's definitions are unusually exact for a book about art. A beat is the smallest unit, an exchange of action and reaction. A scene is an action through conflict, in roughly continuous time and place, that turns the value-charged condition of a character's life. A sequence is a run of scenes, usually two to five, building to a bigger impact. An act is a run of sequences ending in a major reversal. The story climax is the change that cannot be undone.

The key word is turns. By value, McKee means a human charge that can flip: life and death, love and hate, truth and lie, hope and despair. A scene starts with the charge one way and ends with it the other, through an action or a revelation. If a scene ends where it started, it is not a scene. It is exposition wearing a scene's clothes, and it should be cut.

This is a ruthless test and it works on non-fiction too. Take your last presentation or long email and ask of each section: what turns here? If the answer is only that the reader now knows something new, you have written exposition. If the reader's sense of the situation went from safe to threatened, or from stuck to possible, you have written a scene.

He adds the law of diminishing returns. The more often something happens, the less effect it has. The first threat frightens; the fifth bores. So escalation is not optional. Each turn must cost more than the last, or the audience stops registering it. Anyone who has sent a client a fourth identical reminder letter has watched this law at work.

Above the scenes sits what McKee calls the controlling idea: the single sentence a finished story expresses, made of a value and its cause. Not a vague theme like love or justice, but a claim such as justice triumphs because the protagonist is cleverer than the criminal. He distinguishes it from the premise, the open question that starts you writing. The controlling idea is what you discover you have said once you have said it, and a story, or a pitch, that has two or three of them has none.
ch.cap: The letter lands and the scene turns hope to despair

b: McKee separates two things most people blur. Characterisation is everything you can see: age, job, accent, clothes, the way someone holds a glass. True character is what lies underneath, and in ordinary life it cannot be seen at all, because nothing tests it.

His formula is that true character is revealed in the choices a person makes under pressure, and the greater the pressure, the deeper the revelation. The choice must be real, between two things they genuinely want, or between two evils. A decision that costs nothing shows nothing.

This is why most testimonials are useless. They were great to work with is characterisation. We nearly went with the cheaper broker and I had to talk my husband round is character: a choice, under pressure, with something at stake. It is also why the interview question about a hard decision only works when you ask what the candidate gave up.

McKee's deepest point here is that the choice should cost something real. A choice between good and evil is no choice at all, because everyone picks good. A true dilemma is between two goods, or between the lesser of two evils, and that is where the audience leans forward. Notice that this is exactly the situation most of your clients are in when they come to you: choosing between two bad options, under pressure, with their home or their savings at stake.
ch.cap: Two lit doors, one choice, and real pressure

b: McKee's most useful principle for anyone making a case is what he calls the principle of antagonism. A protagonist and the story can only be as fascinating and as moving as the forces against them make them. The audience measures a hero by what the hero beats. Strengthen the opposition and you strengthen the hero for free.
Antagonism need not be a villain. McKee is clear that it can come from people, society, time, space, or any object, alone or all at once. It can be a market, a regulator, a deadline or a debt.

Apply it to any business plan in which the competition is stupid, the regulator is a nuisance and the market is obviously ready. You have just told your audience the opportunity is trivial, because if it were that easy someone would already have done it. The strongest thing you can say about your plan is an honest account of why it is hard.

He goes deeper with what he calls the negation of the negation. Beneath a value and its opposite lies a third, worse level. There is truth, then the lie, and beneath the lie, self-deception, which is worse because the liar at least knows the truth. There is justice, then unfairness, then tyranny, which is injustice made into law. Great stories, he argues, reach that bottom level. Most stop politely at the second.
ch.cap: A small hero against a giant of debt and deadlines

b: In 2002 McKee became a film character. The screenwriter Charlie Kaufman, stuck on a script, wrote a film about a stuck screenwriter called Charlie Kaufman who goes to a Robert McKee seminar. The film was Adaptation, and Brian Cox played McKee as a bellowing oracle. In the best-known scene he thunders that God help you if you use voice-over, in a film that is narrated in voice-over almost throughout.

McKee's response is the best introduction to the man. He said he loved it, that his son told him Cox had nailed him, and his organisation has since used the film in its own marketing. The guru absorbed his own parody and turned it into advertising.

And there is a twist inside the film. Adaptation mocks the formulaic Hollywood ending, then in its final act collapses into exactly that, with drugs, a chase and a death, and it works. Was Kaufman mocking McKee or proving him right? Arguably both. He had learned the rules well enough to break them from the inside.

It also says something about how ideas travel. A line often quoted as McKee's, that stories are equipment for living, is not his. He quotes it in Story as an epigraph, credited to the critic Kenneth Burke, whose essay Literature as Equipment for Living dates from 1938. The credit fell off on the conference circuit, and the more famous name took the sentence. Memory files ideas under whoever is easiest to recall, which is Wednesday's ladder at work on a single line.
ch.cap: On film, the guru bellows; the stuck writer listens

b: Two more of McKee's tools matter for business. The first is subtext. Text is what is said. Subtext is what is really going on: the thoughts and desires people will not or cannot say. In life nothing is quite what it seems, so writing in which everyone says exactly what they mean sounds false. The second is to spend exposition like ammunition. Never have one character tell another something they both know just to inform the audience. Release information at the moment of greatest pressure, keep the best for last, and show rather than announce. A pitch deck that opens with eleven slides of company history and market size has fired its whole magazine into the air before the fight.

In June 2003 the Harvard Business Review published an interview with McKee called Storytelling That Moves People, and it brought his ideas into corporate life. There are two ways to persuade people, he argued. The first is conventional rhetoric: here is our challenge, here are the statistics, here is what we must do. It fails, not because the numbers are wrong, but because statistics invite counter-statistics. An argument summons an opposing argument. The second, much more powerful way is to unite an idea with an emotion, and the vehicle for that is story, which is not a claim to rebut but an experience to go through. His short definition is worth keeping: a story expresses how and why life changes.
He added a warning executives rarely want to hear. Great stories illuminate the dark side. The leader who tells the truth about the obstacle is the one who gets believed about everything else.

For a debt adviser or a broker, this is especially useful. A page that lists features, rates and steps is rhetoric. A page that follows one person from the night they could not open the post, through the moment they picked up the phone, to the morning the letters stopped, is a story. The facts are the same. Only one of them is felt.
ch.cap: In the boardroom a story beats the statistics

b: McKee has many critics. Writers and film scholars have accused him of presenting one historically specific Hollywood form, descended from Aristotle, as if it were the structure of human nature, and of encouraging formulaic films. Some reviewers have been openly scornful of him. His defence is the principles, not rules opening, and the fact that the book does map out quieter, open-ended and fragmented kinds of story alongside the classic plot, though no reader can miss which one he prefers.

Two corrections are worth carrying. He is not the three-act structure man. That label belongs more to the screenwriting teacher Syd Field, and McKee criticises rigid page-count formulas. And the impressive statistics his organisation advertises about famous alumni and awards are marketing, not evidence. Nobody has properly tested whether screenwriting manuals make people better writers.

There is also a fair point in his favour. The principles he teaches about conflict, change and choice are far older than Hollywood. Aristotle described reversals and recognitions in Greek tragedy more than two thousand years earlier, and storytellers in every culture have used them since. McKee's achievement was not to invent these principles but to name them precisely enough to be used on a Tuesday afternoon.

What survives is a set of tools that work far beyond film. Find the gap. Make every section turn. Show character through costly choices. Make the opposition strong. Tell the truth about the dark side. The child actor who learned that audiences only stay for what happens next spent his life explaining why, and his explanation is the best one we have.
ch.cap: On Aristotle's stage, the old principles outlast critics

take: Put a gap in every pitch
Tell one moment when you expected one thing and got another. It holds attention and proves you learned something the hard way.
Ask of every slide, page or paragraph: what changes for the reader here? If nothing does, cut it or rewrite it.
Collect testimonials that describe a hard decision, such as nearly choosing a cheaper option. That reveals character; praise does not.
Describe the competitor, the regulation or the market honestly and at full strength. A hard problem makes your solution impressive.
Do not open with company history. Start where the trouble starts and hold back your strongest fact for the moment it matters.
Pair an idea with an emotion
Statistics invite counter-statistics. Wrap your key number inside a real case of how and why someone's life changed.
Leaders who admit the obstacle are believed about everything else. Lead team updates with the honest problem before the plan.
Learn the rules before breaking them
Kaufman mocked McKee and still used his structure. Master the conventions of your trade before deciding which to ignore.
recall: What is McKee's gap, and why does it matter?

It is the rift between what a character expects when they act and what actually happens. It forces a new, riskier choice and is the only place meaning is produced. A pitch in which everything goes to plan has no gap, so it holds no attention.
What is McKee's test for a real scene?

Whether a value turns. A scene is an action through conflict that flips a value-charged condition, such as hope to despair, through action or revelation. If the value ends where it started, it is exposition and should be cut.
State the principle of antagonism and its lesson for a pitch.

A protagonist and story can only be as compelling as the forces against them. Describing rivals as stupid and markets as easy makes the opportunity look trivial. An honest, strong account of the obstacle makes your plan look stronger.
What is the negation of the negation?

A third level beneath a value and its opposite, worse than the simple negative. Truth, then the lie, then self-deception, which is worse because the liar at least knows the truth. Great stories reach that level.
What did McKee tell the Harvard Business Review in 2003?

That there are two ways to persuade: conventional rhetoric, which invites counter-argument, and uniting an idea with an emotion through story. A story is an experience, not a claim to rebut. He defined it as expressing how and why life changes.
note: Documented: McKee's birth in Detroit in 1941, his Michigan education, his seminar from 1983 onwards, the 1997 book, Adaptation in 2002 with Brian Cox, and the June 2003 HBR interview with Bronwyn Fryer. Accounts differ on how much of the seminar Charlie Kaufman attended, so the narrative does not depend on it. Criticism of McKee as formulaic is widespread among writers and scholars; the source's specific magazine verdicts were not independently checked and are summarised generally. Whether screenwriting manuals improve writing has not been tested.
words: Background information given to an audience so they can follow what is happening.
McKee says a scene that ends where it started is exposition wearing a scene's clothes, and should be cut.
The real meaning or feeling beneath what is actually said.
McKee argues that dialogue in which everyone says exactly what they mean sounds false, because in life the truth sits in the subtext.
Active opposition or resistance, whether from a person or from circumstances.
McKee's principle of antagonism holds that a hero is only as fascinating as the forces against them, which can be a rival, a deadline or a debt.
A short quotation placed at the start of a book or chapter to set its theme.
The line that stories are equipment for living appears in Story as an epigraph credited to Kenneth Burke, though it is often quoted as McKee's own.
A sudden reversal of fortune, the term Aristotle used for a turning point in tragedy.
McKee's insistence that every scene must turn is a modern restatement of the peripeteia Aristotle described in Greek tragedy.
stories: The screenwriter who wrote himself in

Charlie Kaufman was hired to adapt Susan Orlean's book The Orchid Thief for the screen, and he could not do it. So he wrote a film about a blocked screenwriter called Charlie Kaufman trying to adapt The Orchid Thief, gave the character an invented twin brother called Donald, and sent the pair of them into the world of Robert McKee's seminar. The film, Adaptation, came out in 2002. Its final act collapses into the very Hollywood ending it mocks, with drugs, a chase and a death, and it works. The screenplay was nominated for an Oscar, with the fictional Donald credited as co-writer. Mockery or proof? Arguably both.
God help you if you use voice-over

In Adaptation, the actor Brian Cox plays Robert McKee as a bellowing oracle pacing a seminar stage. In the best-known scene he thunders that God help you if you use voice-over, in a film that is narrated in voice-over almost all the way through. Most gurus would have sulked or reached for a lawyer. McKee said he loved it, that his son told him Cox had nailed him, and his organisation has since used the film in its own marketing. The man who teaches that character is revealed by choices under pressure was handed a public parody, and chose to turn it into advertising.

A sentence often quoted on the conference circuit as Robert McKee's is that stories are equipment for living. It is a lovely line, and it is not his. McKee uses it in Story as an epigraph, properly credited to the American critic Kenneth Burke, whose essay Literature as Equipment for Living dates from 1938. Somewhere between the book and the keynote slides, the credit fell off, and the more famous name took the sentence. It is a neat proof of how memory works: ideas get filed under whoever is easiest to recall, not whoever said them first. Always check the footnote before quoting a guru.
biz: McKee says character is revealed by choices under pressure, which is why great to work with tells a reader nothing. When you next ask HomeownersLoan or Debt Support Direct customers for a review, ask a different question: what nearly stopped you going ahead, and what made you decide? Answers like that show a real choice with something at stake. Use only genuine reviews, with the customer's permission, never edited to change their meaning, and keep them balanced so they are not misleading about typical outcomes. Measure whether pages carrying these reviews lift enquiry rates and, more importantly, the share of enquiries that go on to proceed.

McKee told executives that the leader who tells the truth about the obstacle gets believed about everything else. On Debt Support Direct pages, that means putting the downsides of each debt solution, such as the effect on a credit file and the fact that no single solution suits everyone, near the top rather than in small print. Then show how one real client's situation changed, with their written consent and details anonymised, from the night they could not open the post to the morning the letters stopped. Measure enquiries, but also cancellations and complaints, which show whether people understood what they chose.
connects: Ogilvy's story appeal, the eyepatch that makes the mind finish an unfinished tale, is McKee's gap working in a single photograph.
McKee's claim that true character shows only in choices under pressure is the same insight Frankl drew from the camps, where the last freedom was the choice of how to respond.
McKee's view that stories persuade where statistics fail fits Harari's argument that shared stories are what let large numbers of humans cooperate.
recap:
Robert McKee was born in Detroit in nineteen forty-one and was put on a theatre stage as a boy. He learned there, from the inside, the thing he would spend his life explaining. An audience sits still only while it wants to know what happens next.

He studied theatre, acted and directed in New York, began a doctorate he never finished, and moved to Los Angeles to write. His real gift was explaining why stories worked. In nineteen eighty-three he began teaching a course that grew into his Story Seminar, days in a hotel ballroom with a large, ferocious man pacing the stage. In nineteen ninety-seven he set it down in a book, insisting it was about principles, not rules.

The first idea is the gap. A character wants something and acts, expecting the world to respond one way. The world responds differently, usually worse. That rift between expectation and result is where story lives, and it is why a pitch in which every plan simply works is so dull. Attention is not caught by competence. It is caught by surprise.

The second is that every scene must turn. It starts with a value one way, hope or safety or trust, and ends with it the other way. If nothing turns, it is exposition dressed as a scene, and it should be cut. The third is that true character is revealed only by choices made under pressure, and a choice that costs nothing reveals nothing. The fourth is antagonism. A hero is only as impressive as what the hero beats, so be honest about why your task is hard. The fifth is subtext and timing. Spend information like ammunition, at the moment of greatest pressure.

In two thousand and two the screenwriter Charlie Kaufman put McKee into his film Adaptation, played by Brian Cox, bellowing against voice-over in a film full of it. McKee loved it and used it in his own marketing. A year later the Harvard Business Review brought him into the boardroom, where he argued that statistics invite counter-statistics, while a story is an experience to go through rather than a claim to rebut.

His critics say he turned one Hollywood form into a formula, and the alumni statistics his organisation advertises are marketing, not evidence. But the principles he named are as old as Aristotle. His achievement was to name them precisely enough to use.

The line to remember is his own short definition. A story expresses how and why life changes.
